name: general-dynamic-model
title: General Dynamic Model: does island ontogeny make richness hump then decline?
question:
Under the General Dynamic Model of oceanic island biogeography (Whittaker,
Triantis & Ladle 2008), an island's area is not static: it is born, grows as
it is built up, then subsides and erodes over geological time. When area rises
then erodes (island ontogeny), does species richness OVERSHOOT and then
DECLINE — a humped trajectory — unlike the flat static-area MacArthur-Wilson
equilibrium?
hypothesis:
The GeneralDynamicModelProcess uses the same colonization/extinction
bookkeeping as the MacArthur-Wilson process — each of n_pool mainland species
present or absent, colonizing absent species at c = colonization_base and
removing present species at e(t) — but recomputes e(t) each tick from a
time-varying area(t) = area_max*((t/t_peak)*exp(1-t/t_peak))^ontogeny_shape
that rises to area_max at t_peak then erodes. Because extinction falls with
area, the instantaneous equilibrium S*(t) = P*c/(c+e(t)) is itself humped.
Richness chases this moving target with a relaxation lag, so it must rise to an
overshoot while the island is young and large, then decline as the island
erodes — a hump the static MacArthur-Wilson plateau cannot produce. The lag
also makes the richness-vs-area trajectory trace a hysteresis loop (richness
peaks after area and decays more slowly).
objective:
Over a 10-seed ensemble on a focal mid-age island (t_peak = 150), run the
island through 500 model-time units (~3.3 * t_peak) so it is carried well past
its area peak and into erosion. Measure the peak richness, its timing, and the
early- and late-run richness, and confirm the ensemble-mean richness is humped
(peak in the middle third of the run, clearing both the early and late richness
by a clear margin). Render area(t) and richness(t) overlaid, the richness-area
hysteresis loop, and the ensemble trajectory with a variance band.
description:
This study extends the static MacArthur-Wilson equilibrium
(mw-equilibrium-reproduction) with the single ingredient Whittaker, Triantis
& Ladle (2008, citekey whittaker2008general) argue is decisive for oceanic
(volcanic) islands: island ontogeny. The GeneralDynamicModelProcess is
deliberately identical to MacArthurWilsonEquilibriumProcess except that the
island's area traces a humped life-cycle A(t), so the per-species extinction
probability e(t) = extinction_base*(ref_area/A(t))^area_exponent is lowest at
the island's prime and rises again as it erodes. Three islands are staggered
along a t_peak age gradient (120/150/180) so a single run shows young, mid-life
and old islands peaking at different times — the GDM's space-for-time logic.
The headline result is the emergent humped richness trajectory, the GDM's
central qualitative departure from the 1967 equilibrium theory.

expected_behavior.name: richness-is-humped
expected_behavior.en:
Under island ontogeny the ensemble-mean richness rises to a peak in roughly
the middle third of the run then declines: the peak index is neither at the
start nor the end, and peak richness exceeds both the early and late richness
by a clear margin (overshoot-then-decline, not a static plateau).
expected_behavior.condition: peak in middle third AND early < 0.75*peak AND late < 0.75*peak
expected_behavior.rationale:
The GDM's defining prediction is that richness tracks a humped S*(t) driven
by the island's rise-and-erode area, so richness must overshoot and then fall
rather than relax to a flat equilibrium. A peak pinned to the middle of the
run that clears both ends distinguishes a genuine hump from a monotone
approach or a late plateau.

behavior_tests.name: richness-is-humped
behavior_tests.description:
Ensemble-mean richness on the focal island must be humped: peak inside the
middle third of the run, and both the early and late richness below 0.75x the
peak.

provenance.note:
Measured on the focal mid-age island (island_01, t_peak=150), 10-seed
ensemble, 500 model-time units (run length 501 ticks; middle third =
ticks 167-334). Ensemble-mean richness peaks at S = 51.8 at t = 195
(well inside the middle third), rising from an early-run mean of 18.5
(first 10%) and falling to a late-run mean of 26.7 (last 10%) — a
peak/late ratio of 1.94 and peak/early of 2.80. Both ends clear the
0.75*peak = 38.9 margin, so the hump gate passes with room to spare. The
0.75 margin and middle-third window are conservative floors for a visible
overshoot-then-decline.

pipeline_gate.proceed_condition:
Having established that the static MacArthur-Wilson process reproduces the
rate-crossing equilibrium and turnover, adding island ontogeny (time-varying
area) and observing an emergent humped richness trajectory demonstrates the
General Dynamic Model's qualitative departure from the static equilibrium.

canonical_runs.name: default
canonical_runs.label: Area(t) + richness(t) hump, hysteresis loop, 10-seed ensemble trajectory

conclusion:
Adding island ontogeny to the MacArthur-Wilson colonization/extinction process
produces the General Dynamic Model's signature prediction (Whittaker, Triantis
& Ladle 2008): species richness is humped in time, not flat. On the focal
mid-age island (t_peak=150, 10-seed ensemble, 500 model-time units),
ensemble-mean richness rises to a peak of S = 51.8 at t = 195 — comfortably
inside the middle third of the run — then declines to a late-run mean of 26.7
(a ~1.9x drop from the peak) as the island erodes and extinction climbs. The
richness peak lags the area peak and the trajectory decays more slowly than it
rose, tracing a richness-area hysteresis loop. This is exactly the
overshoot-then-decline the static-area MacArthur-Wilson equilibrium (which
relaxes to a single flat S*) cannot generate, confirming that island ontogeny
alone is sufficient to turn the equilibrium plateau into a humped life-cycle
trajectory.

richness-is-humped.detail: peak S=51.8 at t=195 (mid-run); early 18.5, late 26.7 -> clear hump.

findings.statement: Under island ontogeny (area rises then erodes), richness overshoots and then declines (peak ~52 at mid-age, falling to ~27): the MacArthur-Wilson equilibrium is transient over geological time, as the General Dynamic Model predicts (Whittaker 2008).
